name: Gareth Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I direct the theatre pit band, teach drummers on Saturdays and arrange demos when another act calls. My music master’s helps with scores, but show day is mostly making sure players, singers and microphones are ready together.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What keeps you doing it, and what is hardest?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the count-in when the whole room comes with me. I do not love a producer who calls a long rehearsal a favour instead of paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the ensemble that AI can sort a rehearsal calendar, but it still takes players to hold a groove. The theatre should not confuse a tidy rota with a good show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have nearly a year of expenses saved, and the theatre pays me well for music direction. I still keep an eye on ticket sales because a short run means fewer paid nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will keep leading the pit band and my Saturday drum pupils this season. I already use AI now and then for practice schedules, but I will continue checking every part with the players.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the ordinary changes. I have time and a few other theatres nearby if a production closes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the last shortened production cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The last short run cost me two performances, but the teaching income kept the month whole. I would ask the producer what next season is booking before paying for new cymbals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your apprentice do on show night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My apprentice carries cases, sets microphones and hears how a drummer counts a singer in. I pay the apprentice from the show fee because work should be paid.

I would ask the theatre to judge **show quality**, not only a neat rota.
think: My **year of savings** and teaching pay cover a short production run.
I still watch **ticket sales** because they determine paid nights.
do: Keep the **pit band** and Saturday drum pupils this season.
Check my existing **AI schedules** with the players before rehearsal.
Ask the **producer** about next season before paying for new cymbals.
feel: I feel **calm** because savings and teaching income cover ordinary gaps.

fieldNote: His **high pay** and savings cushion a short run without changing jobs.
His occasional **AI use** is existing practice and checked with players, so no learning tag follows.

steps.text: Keep directing the pit band and teaching Saturday drummers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the producer that AI can make demos, draft parts and answer booking emails, but a live band still earns a fee. I would propose a clear rehearsal minimum in the next contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My demo arrangement work may shrink, perhaps a fifth of income in a strong season. I have a cushion, but I do not want the theatre to use cheap tracks to squeeze paid rehearsal hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would put last season’s paid rehearsal hours beside the new contract offer. In the first year I would trial the theatre’s AI part-checker on one score only if another director shows it works, then verify the drum cues myself before a player sees them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about losing a fifth of strong-season income. I could afford a smaller demo year. A thin rehearsal schedule would make the band worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test an AI score checker safely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not take a new tool into a full production on the first day. If the trial misplaces one cue, I would return to the paper score.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exact rehearsal minimum would you ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A minimum of two paid rehearsals before opening would let the band hear the singers. If the producer will not put that in writing, I would ask another theatre about its next show.

Ask **another theatre** about a show if the producer refuses two paid rehearsals.
feel: I feel **anxious** about demo-fee loss and a possible cut to paid rehearsals.
S1.quote: A thin rehearsal schedule would make the band worse.
fieldNote: He distinguishes a manageable **demo loss** from theatre decisions about paid rehearsal time.
His tool trial depends on a **trusted director** and his own check of drum cues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the pit band that AGI by 2028 may make every demo we currently sell, but we should still be paid to play. I would ask the producer for a written season schedule before anyone signs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think demo income goes in 2028, and the theatre may cut arranging and planning hours then. Robots that can play hands-on parts arrive around 2031, so stage work has some time, but no one guarantees the producer keeps a band.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would collect my demo invoices and ask two nearby theatres what their next seasons need. If AGI removes demo fees in 2028, I would keep teaching and use savings for gaps; if this theatre cuts the band, I would apply for an open music-director post before buying new gear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about a lost band contract, but not without a route. A year saved means I can search without making my apprentices work free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your cushion would you keep untouched?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would hold at least six months of expenses untouched. If a contract ends, the other months can fund auditions and travel to the nearby theatres.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my apprentice that I may have fewer show nights, but I would still pay for any night we work. I would not promise dates the producer has not signed.

say: I would ask for a **written season schedule** before signing.
I would insist on **paid show nights** for players and apprentices.
think: My **demo fees** likely end in 2028, before hands-on robots around 2031.
A lost **band contract** would hurt more than the demos.
do: Ask **two nearby theatres** about next seasons this week.
Apply for an **open director post** if the theatre cuts the band after 2028.
Keep **Saturday pupils** after 2028 demo loss, protecting six months of savings and delaying gear until show dates are signed.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a possible lost band contract, with savings to search.
S2.quote: I would not promise dates the producer has not signed.
fieldNote: His **2028 desk-work loss** arrives before the around-2031 stage robot risk.
He protects **six months of savings** and keeps apprentices paid only for confirmed show nights.

steps.text: Apply for an open director post if the pit band is cut
Keep Saturday drum teaching after 2028 demo loss, protecting six months of savings
Delay new gear until the theatre signs show dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre that AGI by 2031 gives us five years to grow paid audiences and train a new band leader. I would offer a paid assistant role if the producer funds it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My demo arrangements likely vanish in 2031, but five years lets me expand the teaching studio if pupils book. Stage robots around 2034 could change live shows, though I cannot guess what audiences would pay to see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next autumn I would open one extra Saturday drum group only if six pupils pay for a full term. If it fills, I would save the added fees; in the first year after 2031 I would keep directing booked shows and compare the teaching income with the missing demos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel anxious about losing demo work unless the new group fills. The longer clock gives me room to prove demand without raiding savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many pupils fund a group and an assistant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six paid pupils cover the studio and an assistant for that hour. If only three enroll, I would keep the private lessons and not hire anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you mentor without a paid assistant post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would mentor a younger player only if the producer funds a paid assistant place. A title on a poster is not a wage.

I would tell the theatre to build **paid audiences** before 2031.

I cannot predict demand for **2034 stage robots**.

feel: I feel **anxious** about lost demos until paid pupils prove the group works.
S3.quote: A title on a poster is not a wage.
fieldNote: He conditions the extra **group class** on six pupils paying for a full term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell younger drummers that AGI by 2036 leaves years to learn a live room and its people. I would ask the theatre to keep a paid apprentice on every production that can afford one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I could have a solid teaching studio and enough saved to refuse a bad theatre contract. Robots around 2039 could copy a drum part, but they do not tell me what a future audience wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From this year I would save a third of each signed theatre fee after paying my assistant. In the first year after 2036 I would check paid band dates against the last three seasons, then take a nearby theatre offer only if it is better and actually signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the next few years, with nearly a year saved and well-paid teaching. I would keep one eye on the theatre contract rather than lose sleep over 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the producer offers fewer signed dates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not count an unsigned season in my savings plan. If the producer offers fewer dates, I would save from the work already paid and keep the six-month floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should your apprentice carry forward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My apprentice should be able to set a mic, count in a singer and send an invoice. Those are the parts of the job I can pass on now.

say: I would ask for a **paid apprentice** where production budgets allow.
I would teach young drummers the **live room** and its people.
think: A stable **teaching studio** may let me refuse poor theatre terms by 2036.
I cannot know how **2039 robots** change ticket buyers.
do: Save one **third of paid fees** after assistant pay, keeping six months of expenses untouched.
Compare **paid band dates** after 2036, then take a better nearby theatre offer only if signed.
feel: I feel **calm** about near-term work and money while watching contracts.
S4.quote: I would not count an unsigned season in my savings plan.
fieldNote: His savings rule counts only **signed paid work** after paying the assistant.
He keeps a **six-month floor** while considering a future theatre move only with a signed offer.

steps.text: Save one third of paid theatre fees after assistant pay, keeping six months untouched

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because demos may go before I know whether the band gets another signed season. A written schedule, paid rehearsals and open posts at nearby theatres would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the assistant when the show runs late. The last player leaving the stage is still working.

headlineQuote: The last player leaving the stage is still working.
portrait: At **27**, Gareth directs a theatre band, teaches drums and arranges demos with a music master’s and nearly a year saved.
He uses **AI occasionally**, testing a new score checker on one piece only after a trusted recommendation.
His **traditional outlook** favours paid apprentices, written contracts and teaching income earned from enrolled pupils.
He protects **savings** while seeking a signed theatre role only if the current band loses work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** may erase demos before Gareth knows whether the theatre renews its band contract.
whatWouldHelp: A **written schedule**, paid rehearsals and open nearby director posts would give Gareth concrete options.
